The Samarangana-sutradhara (XLIX.6-7), early eleventh century, says prasadas to be built in towns (nagara) should be of stone and baked bricks.

items.note: Kramrisch's account of the Hindu temple's piled walls pressed outward from the small Garbhagriha, widening the perimeter with mouldings, fillets, buttresses and projections.

The Hindu temple has strictly no facade; the directions step forth in buttresses and images from the body of the temple, analogous to the layout of divinities on the Vastupurushamandala, with the garbhagriha corresponding to the Brahmasthana.
The name Prasada, a common name for the main temple building, is said to derive from 'sadanam', the settling of bricks in the fire altar (Satapatha Brahmana).

When a Shiva temple is built the bricks invoke the subtle body, the eightfold manifestation of Shiva and the Principles, merged finally in Nishkala Paramashiva; Kramrisch's Shaiva reading of temple fabric.
Foundation rite (Ishtaka-nyasa): the pit is coterminous with the prasada, filled in layers with earth, stone and sand, and the first bricks are laid when one quarter of the pit remains.
Five or nine first bricks are laid following the course of the sun from the east; the Garbhadhana vessel is later deposited on a moulding of the base according to the patron's status.

items.note: Ishtaka is used for brick, stone or wood alike; first stones of stone temples correspond to first bricks; stone temples have no place in Vedic rites.

Besnagar (Bhopal): a solid stone fence belonged to an 'Uttama Prasada' of Vasudeva, only its brick foundation surviving, of which the Garuda pillar with Heliodoros's inscription formed part; the relics date from the 2nd century BC.

Earliest preserved stone temples in central India have unadorned walls of a few courses of large dressed stones joined without mortar and a flat stone roof; stone an accepted material in treatises from the sixth century AD.
Adharashila foundation rite per Tantrasamuccaya and Silparatna: first stone in the middle of the pit, with a treasure jar, stone, silver and gold lotuses and tortoises placed above.
Kramrisch's symbolic reading of the foundation: the square stone Adharashila carries the Shakti vase, stone lotus and tortoise (Vishnu) as the temple's 'support' and stability.
The Adharashila is the omphalos (nabhi) of the temple, the concrete form of universal manifestation, as the navel of the Uttaravedi in the Fire altar.
The deposition of the Garbha, the seed of the temple, is made above the first bricks at levels varying with the donor's status.

items.note: The Mayamata (XV.78; XXV.186-87) allows stone for temples for Brahmanas, Kshatriyas and heretics but not for Vaishyas and Shudras.
Hindu rock-cut sanctuaries came with reticence; the earliest cave sanctuary, at Udayagiri in Central India, dates from about 400 AD.
Mahanirvana Tantra: it is a hundred times more meritorious to give a brick temple than a thatched one, ten thousand times more to give a stone temple; general temple-patronage ideology.
Before quarrying, the sthapati and astrologer go to the quarry and propitiate the spirits in stones, asking them to depart; craft ritual preceding temple building.
Various tests are applied to stone before it is quarried to know its suitability for temples and images; stone is transformed when it becomes temple substance.
Vastushastra designates rock-cut temples as Layana (Samarangana-sutradhara LIX.236).
Footnote: popular etymology of Prasada, from people feeling happy in big buildings ('Prasadas please'), given in the Ishanashivagurudevapaddhati and Silparatna.

items.note: Wooden temples as carved at Barhut (about 100 BC) and as described in the Samarangana-sutradhara (ch. XLIX, after 1000 AD) are hall temples with pillars supporting roofs.
Kramrisch: the entire superstructure of the temple, the Shikhara, has the curves of bending bamboo or light woods in most Hindu temples.
Stone or brick pillars of temples incorporate the proportions of their wooden prototypes, equal in measure or one and a half to twice as wide (Silparatna XXI.118).
Stones are frequently kept in position without cement; iron dowels hold dry masonry at Deogarh and iron clamps are used for wooden joints.
Sudhashila (plaster) and Vajralepa (glue cement and coating) were applied to temples; Vajralepa a hardened glue mixed with other substances.
Earliest preserved dry masonry is the stone facing of Stupa I, Sanchi; earliest historical occurrence of lime mortar is the brick foundation of the Vishnu temple at Besnagar (ASIAR 1913-14).

items.note: Kramrisch: the calm radiance of white temples is extolled in inscriptions; their whiteness expresses sattvika quality and the ascending tendency of the high superstructure.

Footnote: Mandasor inscription (473-74 AD) says the temple 'shines white' like a mountain; Lakshmana temple Khajuraho inscription (VS 1011) praises it as rivalling snow peaks; examples of how inscriptions describe temples.
Stone, brick or wood alike may disappear under a coat of plaster, which might have been coloured too; the material does not guide the builder.

Footnote: how far structural temples were plastered and painted is hard to say; Deccan cave temples were originally plastered and painted; in temples still in worship plaster has been overlaid by whitewash.
Kramrisch: construction forms transfer from one material to another, e.g. bamboo curves copied in bent wood and cut in brick and stone, conveying the same meaning.
